title: Cotton Candy Planets: The Puffiest Worlds Ever Discovered
summary: What if a planet the size of Jupiter had the density of a cloud? That's essentially what astronomers have found: two 'superpuff' planets so lightweight they defy easy explanation. Orbiting the sunlike star TOI 791, about 1,113 light-years away, these worlds are each roughly as wide as Jupiter but with less than 6% of its mass. Their densities — 0.038 and 0.047 grams per cubic centimeter — are on par with cotton candy or shaving foam. The planets were initially detected by NASA's TESS telescope as they transited their star, causing tiny dips in brightness. But determining their mass required a clever approach. The two planets periodically pass close to each other, gravitationally nudging one another. By measuring these orbital kicks, a team led by astrophysicist George Dransfield at the University of Oxford could calculate their masses: about 9.5 and 18.6 times Earth's mass, respectively. Crucial to this measurement was the Antarctic Search for Transiting ExoPlanets (ASTEP) telescope. Because each transit lasts about 12 hours, only Antarctica's months-long winter darkness provided an uninterrupted view. 'Without this telescope, this discovery would not have happened,' Dransfield says. The origin of superpuffs remains mysterious. They may have formed farther out and migrated inward, their atmospheres swelling from the heat. Alternatively, they could be young, still cooling and contracting. Astrophysicist Anthony Piro suggests we might be catching them at an 'intermediate stage.' Future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope will probe their chemical makeup, offering clues about planetary formation and evolution. These fluffy oddities remind us how diverse the cosmos truly is.
why_it_matters: Discovering planets as light as cotton candy challenges our ideas about how planets form and survive. Studying these extremes pushes the limits of atmospheric science and could reveal new processes that shape worlds across the galaxy — maybe even those that might support life.

background_read: NASA's TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has discovered thousands of planet candidates by staring at large areas of the sky and recording the subtle dimming when a planet passes in front of its star. This method, called the transit method, is especially good at finding worlds with tight orbits.

The star TOI 791 is a sunlike star located 1,113 light-years away. Because these planets orbit it closely, they receive intense heat, which may have puffed up their atmospheres — making them some of the lowest-density planets known.

Antarctic astronomy offers a unique advantage: during winter, the sun doesn't rise for weeks, allowing continuous observation of a target. The ASTEP telescope at Dome C, Antarctica, made this discovery possible by tracking the 12-hour-long transits without interruption.

Astrophysicist George Dransfield at the University of Oxford led the team. Fellow astrophysicist Anthony Piro notes that superpuffs might be caught in a young, cooling phase, making them snapshots of planetary evolution not normally seen.

perspectives.description: These fluffball planets are a triumph of modern astronomy. By combining data from space-based and polar telescopes, scientists measured masses and densities that were once impossible to determine — opening a window onto a whole new class of worlds and proving that the universe is even more creative than we thought.

Superpuffs are so fragile that their atmospheres might be eroding quickly under their star's radiation. If they're short-lived, we may be looking at a rare snapshot, and drawing broad conclusions from just two objects could lead to overgeneralization. Their extreme nature also makes them hard to compare to more typical planets.

The study of superpuffs fits into a larger pattern in exoplanet science: the more we look, the more weird planets we find. Systems like TOI 791, with closely spaced, low-density worlds, can act as natural laboratories for testing theories of atmospheric heating, migration, and mass loss that apply across the whole exoplanet population.

As the James Webb Space Telescope turns its spectrographs toward these worlds, we may learn what their atmospheres are made of — water vapor, hydrogen, or something else. That data could confirm or rewrite our models, and in the next decade, similar discoveries might even influence how we search for habitable planets in stranger environments.
